title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: What separates a workflow from an agent?

options.text: In a workflow the model picks each step; in an agent the code fixes the steps in advance
In a workflow the code fixes the steps in advance; in an agent the model picks each step
A workflow never calls a language model at all, while an agent calls one at least once
A workflow makes one tool call in total, while an agent is allowed to make several

items.stem: The makerspace assistant's code always does these steps in this order: search the manuals for the student's question, pass the top three passages to the model, and return the answer the model writes. What is this design?

options.text: An agent, because a language model writes the final answer the student reads
An agent, because it uses a search tool to find passages in the manuals
An agent, because it takes three separate steps instead of a single model call
A workflow, because the code, not the model, fixes the order of the steps

items.stem: A student writes: "Book me any machine that can cut 6 mm acrylic, any time this week." The assistant has calendar, manual-search and booking tools, and after each result it decides which tool to call next, or to stop. Who owns the control flow here?

options.text: The model, because it chooses the next action after seeing each result, so this is an agent
The program, because it is the program that actually runs every tool the model asks for
The developer, because they wrote the tool descriptions that the model reads each time
Neither, because the loop simply repeats until a stopping condition ends it for them

items.stem: After every booking, the assistant must check the student's training status, write the booking to the calendar, and email a confirmation. These three steps are the same every time. Which design fits best?

options.text: An agent, because a model can handle any case and so is always the safer choice
An agent, because a loop that picks each step costs less than the same fixed code
A fixed workflow, because the steps are known in advance, so code can run them predictably and cheaply
A fixed workflow, because code never makes mistakes while an agent will always get something wrong

items.stem: Which of these requests would most justify giving the assistant agent-style control over its steps, rather than a fixed workflow?

options.text: "What are the laser cutter's opening hours?", which is always one lookup in the manual
"Show me my bookings for today", which is always one calendar query then a list
"Cancel my 3 pm booking today", which is always a lookup, a delete and a confirmation
"Find a time this week when a 3D printer and a laser cutter are both free, then book it"

items.stem: At the design review, a teammate says: "Make the whole assistant one agent, since agents are the most capable." With a small model budget, which reply is best?

options.text: Agree, since the model can skip steps it doesn't need, so an agent costs no more than a workflow
Use an agent only where the steps can't be known ahead, since every loop step is another model call and fixed parts run cheaper as workflows
Disagree, since a workflow can't call a model, so it could never answer questions from the manuals
Agree, since a fixed workflow would need rewriting whenever a student words a request differently
